extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Philosophical Transactions: natural philosophers, physicians, geographers, and Royal Society members
extracted.subtask_description: Composing or assessing a 17th-century observational scientific report that includes practical medical remedies, natural-history description of a lake and its fisheries, empirical measurements (blood/circulation), and short book reviews/critique of scientific works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never-failing remedy: Virginia snake-root & St. John's wort
rubrics_metrics.description: Take Virginia snake-root and flowers of St. John's wort, gathered in their prime, equal parts of each; let them be made into very fine powder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dose is from a scruple to a dram, to be taken in any sort of decoction prepared with specifics. To a horse give 2 drachms; to a dog, from one to 1-1/2 drachm; and this before the 9th day after the bite. (Emphasis: administer prior to the 9th day.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rue + Venice treacle + garlic + tin filings in wine (boiled) remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Take leaves of rue, picked from the stalks and bruised, 6 ounces; Venice treacle, garlic peeled and bruised, and fine filings of tin, each 4 ounces. Put them into 4 lb. of Canary or good white wine (or strong ale for hot constitutions) in an earthen vessel well stopped, gently digest or boil in balneo for 4 hours, keeping in the steam; then press and strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dose: from 2 to 3 ounces (or more for some persons) every morning for 8 days. Patient must fast for three hours after it. The dregs remaining after expression must be bound upon the wound, renewing every 24 hours. The 9th day after the bite must not be let slip before this medicine is taken, lest the poison seize the blood too strongly. Must be given cold or only a little warmed. A double quantity may be given to a beast soon after the bite. The remedy was reported repeatedly administered without failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cock-feather test and topical application; wound lancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pluck the feathers from the breech of an old cock, and apply it bare to the wound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prognosis/test: if the cock swells and dies, the patient will do well; if the cock does not die, the dog was not mad. If the wounds are very small, it is proper to open them with a lancet (i.e., perform minor incision to ensure drainage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-plunge and cataplasm remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the patient be nine times plunged in the sea, while he is fasting, as soon as possible after the bite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After plunges, wash the bitten part with a lye of the ashes of oak wood and urine, and apply a cataplasm of good treacle, alliaria (or hedge garlic), rue and salt. Intended as an early, topical plus systemic regimen immediately after bite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electuary regimen (rue, scordium, snake-root, St John's wort, tin, garlic, treacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take dried rue and scordium, of each 2 drachms; Virginia snake-root 1-1/2 drachm, flowers of St. John's wort 3 drachms, fine filings of tin and garlic cut small, each 4 drachms, good treacle 1 ounce; beat and exactly mix together, adding syrup of lemon peels sufficient to make it into an electuary; divide this into 9 equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration: one part to be taken every day, drinking after it a small draught of good strong ale. Walk after it and do not eat till 4 hours after. Use as little syrup of lemon peels as possible; if unavailable, a syrup made of Malaga-wine with sugar may serve. Make up of this electuary 4-1/2 ounces at a time, so the dose may be half an ounce. (Practical regimen with timing, dosing, and alternatives.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification protocol and prohibition on fishing when lake is full
rubrics_metrics.description: When the lake begins to sink, the inhabitants of the town called Oberdorff or Seedorf give notice thereof to all the neighbouring fishermen that are appointed by the several lords having right in this fishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Town people have orders not only to watch the falling away of the water, but likewise to take care that nobody presume to fish in the lake when it is full of water; that being forbidden. (A civic duty/monitoring and prohibition regime tied to water level.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fishing rights, division of catch, methods and safety cautions during drawdown
rubrics_metrics.description: When pits empty, parish clerk tolls a bell; inhabitants (old and young, men and women) go to fishing, sometimes quite naked; fish they catch are divided in halves: one part given to the prince (lord) of the manor, the other half theirs. In some pits fishermen purchase leave from the lord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods vary by pit and speed of drawdown: some pits fished by hand when shallow, some by trawl, some by long net or 'sayne', some with ordinary nets; certain pits require underground entry with lighted torches. Cautions: sudden and swift recession of water (water runs away as a stream a horse can hardly keep pace with) requires nimbleness—fishermen may scarcely get two hauls before the water is gone. Some pits yield crabs exclusively; methods and equipment should match pit characteristics and hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of fishing in spawning pits (Narte & Piauze)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two pits Narte and Piauze are never emptied, but always remain fenny when the rest of the lake is quite dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief: fish lay their spawn there; therefore it is prohibited to fish in them. Note also presence of many horse-leeches in these pits and customary folk remedy for leeches: have another person urinate on the leech to make it let go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrogeological hypothesis explaining the lake's wet-dry cycle and fauna transport
rubrics_metrics.description: There is under the bottom of the lake another subterraneous one, with which it communicates by several holes; there are also some lakes under the mountain Javornik with surface higher than Zirknitz. These upper lakes can run over into the subterraneous ones via passages; channels differ so that some bring fish, some ducks and fish, others only water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory criteria: an adequate explanation must account for (a) the order in which pits empty (higher pits dry first), (b) why some pits bring water only while others carry fish and/or ducks (depends on whether channels open at surface or below surface), and (c) the rapid filling after rains/thunder (thunder-associated sudden inflows). Use of observable indicators (a stone to show lake sinking) and local spring/stream behaviour supports the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating blood quantity in animals and circulation celerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical measurement examples: sheep of 11-1/2 lb alive had 8-1/2 lb blood? (text lists small measured blood quantities in various animals). Injection technique: in a dog injected into jugular a liquor that coagulated the blood and found 6 oz in right ventricle/atrium; suppose 4 oz received at a time by hearts without force; assume 75 pulses per minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational procedure: assume 4 oz per diastole × 75 pulses/min → 4500 diastoles/hour → 18,000 oz transmitted per hour. Assume a man's blood mass proportional to animals measured (a lamb proportion gave ~8 lb blood for a 160 lb man) leading to estimated circulation 63–140 times per hour depending on assumed total blood mass. Caveat: other anatomists estimate total body blood 15–25 lb, producing different results; the author frames his choice as moderate and justifies assumptions from animal dissections and heart measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desiderata for astronomical tables and observational works
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued features in De la Hire's Tabularum Astronomicarum: large tables of longitudes and latitudes of places taken with great exactness; table of right ascensions and declinations of principal fixed stars deduced from new and accurate observations; empirical table of the moon's equations deduced from observations of eclipses; a correction of the moon's motion arising from the sun's anomaly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for evaluating such a work include (a) accuracy and freshness of observational data (longitudes/latitudes, star positions), (b) inclusion of empirically-derived corrections (e.g., lunar equations from eclipses), (c) useful tables for eclipse calculation (solar especially), and (d) attention to observational conditions and refraction effects (e.g., valley/terrain-induced refraction noted by author). Works should justify methodological choices and cite observational provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and manner of felling and barking timber (regional practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the south of England: timber is felled in spring as soon as sap is fully up and then barked after trees are prostrate while sap remains in their bodies. In Staffordshire: timber is barked in spring before felling while trees stand, and not felled until the following winter when sap is in repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: choice of felling time and whether to bark before or after felling depends on regional custom and preferred timber condition (sap-up bark-after vs. bark-before and winter-fell). These differences affect drying, sap content, and work scheduling; practitioners should follow the method suited to local conditions and intended timber use.
